extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary theory, creative writers, and scholars interested in Russian Formalism and Viktor Shklovsky
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Viktor Shklovsky's formalist principles (notably ostranenie/defamiliarization and fabula/syuzhet) to the production and analysis of creative writing, and to film/screenwriting. Emphasizes devices that slow recognition, experiment with form, and foreground perceptual processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ostranenie (defamiliarization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shklovsky developed the concept of ostranenie or defamiliarization (also translated as 'estrangement') in literature; explained in the essay 'Art as Technique' (1917) and Theory of Prose (1925).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use techniques that 'enstrange' familiar objects and conventions so they are perceived afresh. The page quotes Shklovsky: "And so, in order to return sensation to our limbs, in order to make us feel objects, to make a stone feel stony, man has been given the tool of art." Apply devices that prevent automatic recognition and force readers into renewed perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make perception long and 'laborious' (prioritize perceptual process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shklovsky: 'The perceptual process in art has a purpose all its own and ought to be extended to the fullest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design form and technique to slow down recognition—complicate form, foreground sensory detail, and extend the reader's perceptual engagement. The article adds: 'By "enstranging" objects and complicating form, the device of art makes perception long and "laborious."' Also: 'The artifact itself is quite unimportant.' This suggests valuing the reader's experience/process over mere plot outcomes or artifact status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn the over-familiar into the revitalized (avoid cliché)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shklovsky argued for the need to turn something that has become over-familiar, like a cliché in the literary canon, into something revitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively identify clichés, routinized perceptions, or stock devices and rework them so they are perceived anew—through altered perspective, fresh sensory detail, formal disruption, or surprising presentation. Anti-pattern: relying on recognition or formulaic usage that induces automatic reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabula / Syuzhet (story vs plot distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shklovsky contributed the story/plot distinction (fabula/syuzhet), which separates the sequence of events the work relates (the story, or fabula) from the sequence in which those events are presented in the work (the plot, or syuzhet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reordering, temporal manipulation, and presentation strategies intentionally: the order you present events (syuzhet) can be a device to defamiliarize, create suspense, highlight perception, or control how the reader experiences cause and consequence. Evaluation: distinguish what 'happened' from how the narrative presents it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation with form (semi‑autobiographical disguise, digressive style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shklovsky wrote semi-autobiographical works disguised as fiction that served as experiments in his developing theories of literature; his style was influenced by Laurence Sterne's digressive style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage formal experimentation—hybrid genres, semi-autobiographical masking, digressions, and playful narrative voice—as deliberate devices to alter perception and test theoretical approaches. Example tactic: adopt digressive, non-linear, or hybrid modes to challenge reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply formalist devices to film and screenwriting
rubrics_metrics.description: Shklovsky was an early serious writer on film (Literature and Cinematography) and worked as a screenwriter; he applied formalist thinking to cinematographic practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In film/screenwriting, translate formalist techniques (defamiliarization, manipulation of presentation order, formal complication) into cinematic devices—editing, shot composition, mise-en-scène, narrative sequencing—to make cinematic perception deliberate and renewed. The page notes his essays on film and his collaborations with filmmakers (e.g., Sergei Eisenstein) as context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider literary activity as social practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Shklovsky's work pushes Russian Formalism towards understanding literary activity as integral parts of social practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating creative work, account for the social and historical functions of literary devices and forms—how formal choices interact with social context, circulation, and cultural meaning. Use formal analysis in dialogue with social practice rather than as purely autonomous formal play.
